papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context‑Aware Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students that retain much of the teachers' predictive power. When combined with representation matching, architecture-aware alignment, pre-training of compact models, and appropriate data strategies, KD reliably improves inference efficiency while preserving accuracy in many vision and language tasks. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle limited or heterogeneous data and fairness constraints. Pragmatic deployment therefore treats KD as a first‑line method that must be adapted to task, data, and resource constraints rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from large teacher models to smaller students to reduce inference cost while retaining performance. A broad family of approaches—from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate-feature imitation, multi-teacher ensembles, data-free synthesis, and federated or privacy-aware protocols—enables deployment across vision, speech, and language tasks. Practical success depends on matching the distillation signal to student capacity, combining KD with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, pretraining), and addressing data, optimization, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Recipe
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the first-line, practical strategy for compressing large models in deep learning and NLP because it provides a flexible set of mechanisms to transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from high-capacity teachers to smaller, efficient students. KD recovers much of teacher performance while reducing latency and memory footprint, and it composes naturally with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data synthesis). However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on what is distilled, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability, and robustness under domain shift or privacy constraints. A productive deployment strategy treats KD as the core of a hybrid pipeline, applies task-aware signal selection and layer alignment, uses multi- or student-aware teachers when appropriate, and combines distillation with lightweight model design and compression primitives to meet real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a unifying, practical framework to compress large deep models into smaller, deployable students while addressing concerns of computation, privacy, robustness, and limited task data. KD techniques span from logits- and feature-based matching to progressive module replacement, multi-teacher ensembles, data-free (zero-shot) synthesis, and federated output-sharing, and when combined with careful data augmentation and generative replay they yield compact models that retain much of the teacher utility in real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller ones by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from a teacher to a student. Over the past decade KD methods have diversified beyond simple logit matching to include intermediate-feature imitation, multi-teacher pipelines, data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression. Empirical work across NLP, speech, vision-language, and other domains shows KD can preserve most of a teacher's performance while drastically reducing model size and latency. Theoretical and empirical analyses have clarified why KD works in many settings (regularization via soft targets, ensemble-induced dark knowledge, and representation enrichment), but open problems remain in data privacy, distribution shift, automated student design, and guarantees for out-of-distribution robustness.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become practical tools to reduce model size and computation while retaining much of the performance of large teachers. Across vision, speech, and natural language tasks, approaches include transferring soft logits, mimicking internal features or attention maps, layering/structural adaptations, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-preserving methods. Empirical results demonstrate that careful distillation can yield compact students that approach teacher accuracy and enable deployment in resource-constrained settings, but open challenges remain in robustness, task-specific distillation design, and distributed training dynamics.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential but Context‑Dependent Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied deliberately—choosing which teacher signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacity and inputs, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques—KD routinely delivers large reductions in model size and latency while preserving most task performance. Real-world success requires representation-aware objectives, options for data-limited or privacy-sensitive settings, and careful evaluation under distribution shift and modality-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression methods transfer knowledge from larger, high-capacity models to smaller, efficient models to reduce inference cost and memory while preserving performance. Approaches span soft-label (logit) matching, feature- or attention-level imitation, multi-teacher fusion, data-free distillation, and adaptations for domain shift and heterogeneous deployment. Empirical results show distilled students can approach or match teacher performance in many settings, but success depends on teacher quality, the form of transferred knowledge, training curricula, and application-specific design choices. Emerging theoretical and empirical analyses clarify when and why distillation helps and reveal practical tradeoffs such as bias–variance effects of soft labels and the roles of ensemble and self-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models to emulate larger teacher models so deployments meet latency, memory, or privacy constraints. KD encompasses a spectrum of signals to transfer—including softened outputs, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure—and integrates with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to produce efficient models. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often preserves large portions of teacher performance and can improve student generalization beyond mere compression, but outcomes depend strongly on what is distilled, teacher–student compatibility, access to data, and optimization choices. Practical pipelines therefore combine signal design, data strategies, and task-aware architecture choices to balance efficiency, robustness, and retained performance; open problems remain in data-free and privacy-preserving distillation, principled teacher design, and reliably transferring robustness and rare-token fidelity in sequence tasks.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and selected internal information from teacher models. KD methods range from matching softened teacher logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure, and are commonly combined with complementary engineering strategies (architecture design, pretraining of compact models, quantization, and data augmentation). Empirical evidence shows distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision and language tasks while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability and augmentation, and the relative strength and role of the teacher; these choices shape practical tradeoffs in robustness, fairness, and cross-distribution generalization.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students while preserving much of the teacher’s performance. When combined with complementary techniques—task-adaptive architecture search, representation-level objectives, data- or generator-based synthesis, and careful teacher-student co-design—KD yields compact models that meet real deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy) across vision and NLP. Properly designed distillation pipelines address many practical barriers to deployment while acknowledging and mitigating risks such as transferred biases, teacher–student mismatch, and data scarcity.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a heuristic into a central, practical toolkit for compressing large models and transferring behavior from high-capacity teachers into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative modeling, practitioners combine soft-label supervision, intermediate-representation matching, data- and privacy-aware strategies, and architecture-aware choices to trade accuracy for latency, memory, and power. KD is effective when paired with complementary techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, synthetic-data generation, curriculum schedules), but its success depends critically on what form of knowledge is distilled, how data or augmentations are used, and how teacher–student capacity and domain mismatches are managed. Remaining challenges include robust data-free distillation, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, mitigating bias transfer, and firm theoretical characterizations that predict when and how distillation will work in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches to Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce smaller, faster models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teachers to compact students. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed diverse strategies—teacher–student logits matching, layer-wise representation matching, adversarial sample generation, progressive module replacement, many-to-many layer mapping, and task-aware filtering—to address capacity gaps, data access limits, privacy constraints, and robustness needs. Practical deployments additionally combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, and federated protocols to meet hardware and communication budgets. Empirical work shows that careful design of distillation objectives and inputs can preserve most of the teacher’s accuracy and even transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, while specialized schemes enable distillation without original training data or across continual/heterogeneous settings.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques transform large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, methods include soft-target (logit) distillation, feature and representation matching, layer-mapping strategies for large pretrained models, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and training-time variants such as online or co-distillation. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often retain much of teacher performance while yielding substantial savings in memory, latency, and energy; however, outcomes depend on teacher–student compatibility, access to task data, which signals are transferred, and training protocol choices. Key open problems include robust cross-domain transfer, handling teacher errors and low-frequency phenomena, and reducing distillation cost when teachers are large or data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: West
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Primary, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile method for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. When applied thoughtfully—choosing appropriate distillation signals (logits, features, attention), accounting for teacher–student capacity, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques—KD reliably reduces memory, compute, and latency burdens while enabling deployment across edge, federated, and privacy-sensitive settings. However, KD is not a universal cure: its benefits depend on optimization, data availability, and robustness/fairness goals, and practical deployments require matching KD variants to constraints and verifying student behavior under distribution shift and adversarial threats.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. KD encompasses multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure) and can be adapted to settings with limited or no access to original training data, heterogeneous or federated deployments, and domain-specific constraints. Best outcomes arise when distillation is combined with task-aware student design, appropriate distillation targets, and data or augmentation strategies matched to deployment needs.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, generation, and specialized domains show that KD can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling substantial improvements in latency, memory footprint, and privacy-sensitive deployment. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success hinges on choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention, relational signals), how to align teacher and student representations, how to handle limited or private data, and whether robustness or task-specific constraints must be preserved. Treating KD as a pipeline and co-designing teacher, student, objectives, and data/augmentation yields the most reliable practical gains.

papers_seen.author: Warner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical First-Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically proven approach for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while preserving much of task performance. KD methods—ranging from soft-label matching to feature- and layer-level alignment, multi-teacher and online variants, and data-free techniques—enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, distillation has well-documented failure modes (e.g., propagation of teacher errors, optimization mismatch) that require careful teacher/student design, data strategies, and complementary methods to get reliable results in practice.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied deliberately — choosing what to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacity, and handling data- and deployment-specific constraints — KD yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, distillation is not automatic: outcomes depend on teacher strength and training, student architecture and capacity, the form of distilled signals, data availability (including data‑free settings), and fairness/privacy goals. Best practice treats KD as a core component combined with architecture-aware design, data strategies, and deployment-aware procedures to produce reliable, efficient models for real applications.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression strategies have become central tools for shrinking large pretrained models into efficient deployable networks while preserving much of their performance. Methods range from transferring final-logit 'dark knowledge' to matching intermediate representations, attention maps, or feature distributions; from engineering compact student architectures to progressively replacing modules inside a single model. Applications span vision, speech, generative models, and NLP (including BERT compression and non-autoregressive translation), and extensions address scenarios with no access to original training data or heterogeneous, federated settings. Key trade-offs involve accuracy vs. size/latency, robustness and fairness, and the distributional assumptions needed for effective transfer. Important open problems include principled understanding of when and why distillation helps, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and reliably transferring robustness and inductive biases to small models.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Over the past decade KD has branched from simple soft-target matching into a family of methods including logits and feature matching, layer-wise and task-aware distillation, self- and online-distillation, data-free or adversarial sample synthesis, and strategies for low-precision or few-shot deployment. Practical success depends on matching the distilled signal to student capacity, handling limited or private data, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and combining distillation with complementary compression tools (e.g., pruning and quantization). Open challenges remain around robust data-free distillation, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, preventing harmful bias transfer, and building stronger theoretical predictions of when and how distillation succeeds.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression — Powerful but Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, empirically validated strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD works through a range of mechanisms (soft targets, intermediate representation matching, teacher ensembles, and data‑side interventions) and is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and careful attention to teacher–student alignment, data provenance, and deployment constraints. While KD often yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs, practitioners must treat it as a context‑sensitive tool and follow best practices to avoid transferring undesirable behaviors or encountering failure modes under limited data, heterogeneity, or privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted set of techniques for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students that retain much of the teachers' performance. Modern KD extends beyond soft-label matching to include representation-level objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, data-free or zero-shot variants, and architecture-aware combinations with pruning, quantization, and search. KD has been applied successfully across domains — including language generation, ranking, detection, and federated settings — but its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to manage data, privacy, and distributional shift. Practical deployment requires selecting distillation signals and training regimes that match student capacity and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Mckee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and distributed settings KD often recovers much of a teacher's predictive performance while enabling faster inference, lower memory use, and deployment under resource or privacy constraints. However, KD is not a panacea: outcomes depend on what signals are transferred (logits, features, attention), teacher–student compatibility, availability and quality of data (including data-free or federated setups), and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Best practice treats distillation as one element of a compression pipeline that combines representation matching, architecture-aware student design, data strategies, and risk-aware training protocols.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A spectrum of distillation signals—soft logits, intermediate features and attention, relational/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher ensembles, and data- or privacy-aware synthesis—enables compact models that often retain most of teacher performance. Empirical results across NLP, speech, graph learning, and vision show KD’s practical value, while theoretical and empirical analyses point to mechanisms (soft-target regularization, ensemble-induced ‘‘dark knowledge’’, and representation shaping) and to limits tied to student capacity, data alignment, optimization dynamics, and robustness under distribution shift. Practical deployment requires careful selection of what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design).

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models to reproduce useful behavior of larger teacher models so that deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints becomes practical. KD encompasses a family of techniques — from matching teacher output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure — and is commonly combined with complementary compressions such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows that, when matched to student capacity and data availability, distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Practical success depends on choices about which signals to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data access (including data-free alternatives), and robustness or fairness requirements; remaining challenges concern principled objective design, optimization under capacity mismatch, and reliable transfer of robustness and rare-token/long-tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central to deploying deep models under resource constraints. Methods extend beyond simple logit matching to include intermediate-layer supervision, feature mimicking, projector-based transforms, teacher-student co-training, and data- or domain-aware schemes. Distillation has been applied across modalities (vision, language, multimodal, graphs) and in settings with limited or no access to original training data. Practical advances address transfer across architectures, task-adaptive compression, and efficient architecture search, while open problems remain around distribution shift, heterogeneity of data or detectors, and preserving rare or low-frequency information.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Cobb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. KD transfers information beyond hard labels — including softened output distributions, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational signals — and is commonly combined with architectural or numerical compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest performance loss when teacher–student design, data availability, and optimization dynamics are considered; however, its success is contingent on capacity alignment, data choices, and safeguards against transferring undesirable behaviors. Applications range from accelerated inference and edge deployment to domain adaptation, federated learning, and task-specific adaptations such as non-autoregressive translation and graph-to-MLP compression.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Backbone of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) unifies many successful strategies for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones that retain most of their performance. KD methods are adaptable across settings—from single-task NLP compression to large-scale distributed training and federated learning—and recent advances address core challenges such as teacher-student alignment, multi-teacher fusion, data scarcity, and domain shift. By combining architectural mapping, task-aware selection of distilled signals, dynamic teacher weighting, and online or data-free schemes, KD enables deployment of strong models in latency-, compute-, and privacy-constrained settings while exposing clear directions for further research.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, high-impact approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. KD succeeds because it can transfer diverse forms of information—soft outputs, internal representations, relational structure—and because it composes naturally with complementary techniques (pretraining, pruning, quantization, data augmentation, and multi-teacher ensembles). When applied with attention to teacher quality, data alignment, and student pretraining, KD enables practical, resource-aware deployments across vision, speech, and language tasks. This paper argues KD should often be the first method considered for compression, and outlines core mechanisms, practical recipes, and remaining challenges for robust application in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. KD’s strengths arise from its flexibility in what and how information is transferred (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention, or relational signals) and from its ability to combine with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data augmentation). When applied with attention to teacher–student alignment, distilled signals, and data constraints, KD reliably improves accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across modalities. However, KD is not universally sufficient: success requires careful method selection, handling of distributional and data limitations, and, in some cases, adversarial or privacy-aware extensions.

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Multi-Strategy Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When applied thoughtfully—combining logits transfer, intermediate representation matching, teacher optimization, and data strategies—KD enables substantial reductions in size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student design, the availability and nature of data, robustness and fairness considerations, and the distillation objectives chosen. Best outcomes come from treating KD as one element of a broader compression pipeline that includes architecture choices, augmentation or data-synthesis techniques, and explicit attention to transfer limits.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or more complex models to smaller ones to reduce inference cost, improve deployability, or impart desirable properties (robustness, fairness, interpretability). Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, ensemble consensus, attention maps) and in what data is available (original training data, synthetic data, or no data). Practical systems combine KD with architecture-level compression (pruning, structured sparsity) and with training-time strategies (online or continual distillation, curriculum schedules) to trade off efficiency and accuracy. While KD yields strong empirical results across NLP, speech, vision, and generative models, open challenges remain in data-free settings, cross-domain generalization, preserving fairness and interpretability, and designing distillation objectives that best capture the teacher’s knowledge for a given task.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context‑Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a multifaceted approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with attention to which signals are transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention), the teacher–student relationship, data availability, and deployment constraints, KD yields substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher behavior. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on capacity alignment, data and distributional match, and careful objective design. Practical adoption therefore requires selecting KD variants that fit task and system constraints and combining KD with complementary techniques (pretraining, data augmentation, multi-teacher signals, or architecture co-design) to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multi‑Strategy, Practical — but Bounded — Path for Compressing Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision and language tasks. When applied thoughtfully — combining soft-label transfer with representation-level guidance, architecture-aware design, and data strategies — KD enables compact models that meet memory, latency, and deployment constraints while retaining most of a teacher’s performance. However, KD is not a universal remedy: limited or private data, teacher errors, student capacity gaps, and robustness or fairness concerns create concrete failure modes that require complementary methods and careful evaluation. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a multi-strategy engineering approach whose best results arise from combining several targeted techniques that suit task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods have become central tools for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy and capabilities of large teachers. Research over the past decade has produced a diverse set of techniques—ranging from distilling logits, internal representations, and attention patterns to data-free and few-shot strategies, multi-teacher ensembles, and task-adaptive search for student architectures. These approaches have been applied across vision, language, multimodal, and deployed/distributed settings, demonstrating substantial gains in inference speed and model size while exposing trade-offs in robustness, data requirements, and modality alignment. This survey summarizes the main algorithmic families, common engineering strategies, notable empirical outcomes, and key open challenges for applying distillation in practice.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large deep models into compact ones that are suitable for deployment. Across NLP, speech, vision-language, and specialized tasks such as machine reading comprehension, KD enables students to inherit performance-critical behaviors from larger teachers while enabling orders-of-magnitude reductions in model size and compute. When combined with complementary techniques (e.g., architecture search or structured pruning) and when tailored to task or domain specifics, distillation yields compressed models that approach teacher performance while meeting resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: Principled Use of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, practical method for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while retaining much of teacher performance. However, its success is conditional: choices about what to transfer, how to supervise internal representations, how to design student architectures for particular tasks, and how to handle data, distribution shift, and fairness constraints materially affect outcomes. I argue that KD should be treated as a flexible design pattern—combining soft-target transfer, internal-representation matching, task-adaptive architecture design, and explicit fairness or data strategies—to produce reliable, deployable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Treated as a toolbox rather than a single loss term, KD delivers meaningful efficiency gains across modalities when the distillation targets, student design, and data strategy are chosen for the deployment constraints. However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis methods, and robustness to distribution shift. Practical success therefore requires combining KD with complementary compression techniques, carefully selecting what to transfer, and evaluating students under realistic deployment conditions.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information from one or more teachers. Across vision and language applications, KD has been adapted to handle teacher-free scenarios, multi-teacher setups, intermediate representation alignment, data- and domain-shift, and task-specific constraints such as ranking or retrieval. Empirical work shows that distillation can preserve much of teacher performance while dramatically reducing model size and latency, but practical success depends on what is transferred (soft outputs, internal features, or relational/contrastive knowledge), the quality and heterogeneity of teacher data, and training design choices such as data augmentation and curriculum. The literature also highlights cases where naive distillation propagates teacher errors (e.g., low-frequency lexical mistakes) and where alternative strategies (label smoothing view, internal representation matching, dynamic teacher weighting, or curriculum selection of examples) yield measurable improvements. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, common pitfalls, and promising methods for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students while preserving much of the teacher’s performance. When combined with complementary techniques—task-adaptive architecture search, representation-level objectives, data- or generator-based synthesis, and careful teacher-student co-design—KD yields compact models that meet real deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy) across vision and NLP. Properly designed distillation pipelines address many practical barriers to deployment while acknowledging and mitigating risks such as transferred biases, teacher–student mismatch, and data scarcity.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment in constrained environments. Advances across task-adaptive compression, data-free and zero-shot distillation, multi-teacher and meta-learned teaching, and self-distillation demonstrate KD's broad applicability. However, KD is not a panacea: success depends on data availability, the teacher–student optimization dynamics, and explicit design choices around architecture and training signals. Combining pre-training of compact models, task-aware architecture search, and sophisticated distillation protocols yields the best trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and privacy.
