papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: The Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their performance. KD is applicable across modalities and tasks, from machine translation and reading comprehension to distributed training and privacy-sensitive deployment. Success depends on aligning teacher and student representations, selecting appropriate knowledge (logits, intermediate features, attention, contrastive signals), and matching methods to constraints such as limited data, heterogeneous devices, or privacy requirements. Theoretical analyses and practical advances both show that careful design choices — including attention-based matching, layer projection, task-aware filtering, online collaboration, multi-teacher weighting, and privacy-aware perturbation — materially affect outcomes and trade-offs between fidelity, efficiency, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: West
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Primary, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile method for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. When applied thoughtfully—choosing appropriate distillation signals (logits, features, attention), accounting for teacher–student capacity, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques—KD reliably reduces memory, compute, and latency burdens while enabling deployment across edge, federated, and privacy-sensitive settings. However, KD is not a universal cure: its benefits depend on optimization, data availability, and robustness/fairness goals, and practical deployments require matching KD variants to constraints and verifying student behavior under distribution shift and adversarial threats.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, expressive models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple logit-matching to a diverse toolkit that includes feature- and layer-level supervision, multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, self-distillation and teacher optimization, and approaches that enable data-free or privacy-preserving compression. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling faster inference and smaller footprints; however, practical success depends on choices about objectives, alignment between teacher and student, data availability, and robustness to domain shift. Open directions include stronger theoretical characterization of what is transferred, principled treatment of heterogeneous teachers, and tighter integration of KD with quantization, pruning, and privacy mechanisms.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single logit-matching trick into a versatile, task- and deployment-aware toolkit that can produce compact models with strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. By transferring soft targets, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals, and by integrating with architecture search, data augmentation, and heterogeneous-teacher setups, KD enables practical compression across vision and language modalities. This paper argues KD should be a first-line technique for model compression in deep learning and NLP, describes the complementary methods that make it effective in production settings, and highlights common pitfalls and practical remedies for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer information from larger, often over-parameterized teacher models into smaller, more efficient students to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD strategies vary in what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate representations, relations), how it is transferred (logit matching, feature-mimicking, projector layers, contrastive objectives, adversarial losses), and in deployment settings (data-available, data-free, federated or distributed, and online). Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, distilled students frequently recover much of teacher performance while enabling practical gains in speed and memory; however, method choice, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and distributional shifts materially affect outcomes, and open problems remain in preserving rare-token behavior, transferring robustness and fairness, and compressing across heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Compact, Robust Deep Models: Effectiveness, Limits, and Design Principles
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD succeeds when its design (what to transfer, how, and with which data) is matched to deployment constraints: transferring logits, intermediate representations, or relational signals; using multi- or adaptive-teacher schedules; and combining distillation with model- and data-level compression. However, KD is not a panacea — optimization gaps, mismatched inputs or teachers, and inappropriate sample selection can degrade results — so robust application requires careful teacher-student co-design, selective supervision, and complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: Synthesizing Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies transfer information from larger, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient students so that deployed systems meet latency, memory, or privacy constraints. The literature frames KD as a family of mechanisms — soft-target supervision, intermediate-representation matching, relation- or attention-based transfer, and data-side interventions — that can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance across vision and language tasks, but practical success depends on teacher quality, data availability and augmentation, architecture compatibility, and robustness considerations.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Backbone for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically effective paradigm for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied thoughtfully—choosing what form of teacher knowledge to transfer, aligning teacher and student representations, and combining distillation with other compression tools—KD enables substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of the original model's performance. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on capacity matching, the choice of distilled signals, data availability, and optimization design. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a central tool to be combined with architecture-aware choices and task-specific adjustments to meet real deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their predictive power. Across vision, language, and generative settings, KD extends from simple softened-logit matching to richer objectives that mimic intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure; it also supports varied training regimes including offline teacher–student, online co-training, multi-teacher curricula, and data-free synthesis. When combined with complementary methods (pretraining, architecture search, pruning, quantization, and federated procedures), KD helps meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints in real deployments. However, success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align architectures, how to handle limited or absent data, and how to avoid transferring undesirable teacher behaviors—issues that remain active research directions.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Methods and Challenges in Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models to smaller, faster student models. Across vision, generative modeling, and NLP, researchers have developed logit- and feature-level distillation, task-specific adaptations, multi-teacher schemes, and teacher-optimization strategies to improve student accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. Work also focuses on constraints arising in distributed and privacy-preserving settings, on preserving rare or fine-grained information, and on adapting distillation to complex tasks such as detection, generation, and dense prediction. Practical systems combine architectural choices, training curricula, and distilled supervision to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression approaches transfer information from larger, high-capacity models to smaller, deployable students or otherwise reduce model complexity while preserving task performance. Across vision and NLP, practitioners use a range of supervision signals and training protocols—soft-target matching, feature and attention imitation, representation-level objectives, self-distillation, online co-training, and data-free generation—to trade off accuracy, latency, and resource constraints. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation signals and training recipes can produce compact models that approach teacher performance, but success depends on student capacity, data availability, and alignment between teacher signals and downstream tasks. Open challenges include robust transfer of rare-token behavior, principled selection of what to distill, and scaling distillation to privacy-sensitive or distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Freeman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Toolkit for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an adaptable, empirically validated approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher’s effectiveness. When treated as a flexible toolkit rather than a single loss, KD supports a range of transfer targets (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps), training regimes (single- and multi-teacher, online, data-free), and integrations with complementary compression techniques. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher–student compatibility, access to appropriate data (or metadata), and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Best practice treats distillation as part of an end-to-end compression pipeline that explicitly addresses alignment, data constraints, and downstream task objectives.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become practical tools to reduce model size and computation while retaining much of the performance of large teachers. Across vision, speech, and natural language tasks, approaches include transferring soft logits, mimicking internal features or attention maps, layering/structural adaptations, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-preserving methods. Empirical results demonstrate that careful distillation can yield compact students that approach teacher accuracy and enable deployment in resource-constrained settings, but open challenges remain in robustness, task-specific distillation design, and distributed training dynamics.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a central strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher’s predictive power. A variety of mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate feature imitation, layer- or module-level mappings, and architecture-aware search—enable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, model size, and privacy. Practical deployments combine distillation with complementary methods (pretraining of compact architectures, pruning/quantization, data augmentation, and privacy-preserving synthesis) and tailor choices to data availability, task constraints, and target hardware. Despite broad empirical success, open issues remain around transferring robustness and rare-token behavior, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing distillation pipelines that are robust under limited or private data.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses information from larger, often more expensive teacher models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. Research over the past decade has developed a spectrum of KD objectives (soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, contrastive and relational losses), training regimes (offline teacher-student, online co-training, self-distillation, multi-teacher schedules), and deployment-aware integrations (pre-training students, architecture-aware adapters, and combination with pruning or quantization). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance while reducing parameter count and latency, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and the choice of what and how to transfer. Ongoing challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, matching heterogeneous architectures, preserving low-frequency or domain-specific signals, and automating trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under memory, latency, or privacy constraints. The literature has converged on a set of recurring methods (soft-target/logit supervision, intermediate feature and attention matching, multi-teacher schedules, data-free and privacy-aware protocols) and deployment practices (combining KD with pruning, quantization, or architecture search). Empirical evidence demonstrates that appropriately designed distillation pipelines often recover a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional alignment. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors (especially in NLP), and principled teacher–student co-design and curricula for difficult tasks.

papers_seen.author: Murphy

KD is not a universal cure: limits arise from optimization mismatches, teacher quality, data scarcity, and robustness concerns, so careful design and evaluation are required.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques transfer behaviors of large models into smaller, more efficient models by supervising students with information derived from teachers (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention, or synthetic labels). Empirical results across vision, speech, and language show that carefully designed distillation pipelines can preserve much of a teacher’s performance while reducing size and latency. Effective practice combines choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data strategies (including augmentation or synthesis), and complementary structural compression. Remaining challenges include handling imperfect teachers, limited or private data, robustness and out-of-distribution behavior, and principled automation of trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Compressing Visual-linguistic Model via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite exciting progress in pre-training for visual-linguistic (VL) representations, very few aspire to a small VL model. In this paper, we study knowledge distillation (KD) to effectively compress a transformer-based large VL model into a small VL model. The major challenge arises from the inconsistent regional visual tokens extracted from different detectors of Teacher and Student, resulting in the misalignment of hidden representations and attention distributions. To address the problem, we retrain and adapt the Teacher by using the same region proposals from Student's detector while the features are from Teacher's own object detector. With aligned network inputs, the adapted Teacher is capable of transferring the knowledge through the intermediate representations. Specifically, we use the mean square error loss to mimic the attention distribution inside the transformer block and present a token-wise noise contrastive loss to align the hidden state by contrasting with negative representations stored in a sample queue. To this end, we show that our proposed distillation significantly improves the performance of small VL models on image captioning and visual question answering tasks. It reaches 120.8 in CIDEr score on COCO captioning, an improvement of 5.1 over its non-distilled counterpart; and an accuracy of 69.8 on VQA 2.0, a 0.8 gain from the baseline. Our extensive experiments and ablations confirm the effectiveness of VL distillation in both pre-training and fine-tuning stages.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP

When combined with architecture-aware transformations, feature-level supervision, multi-teacher signals, and careful handling of data constraints, KD enables compact students that retain most of a teacher's effectiveness while meeting latency, memory, and domain requirements. However, distillation artifacts and data limitations require methodic choices—e.g., feature mimicking, confidence-aware multi-teacher weighting, or generative replay—to avoid propagating teacher errors or overfitting in low-data regimes.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Research spans algorithmic advances in teacher–student objectives, architecture-aware compression, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Practical work shows gains from combining KD with data augmentation, many-to-many layer mappings, and architecture search, while complementary efforts address data-free and privacy-preserving distillation. Remaining challenges include imperfect teachers, data heterogeneity, and adapting compression to task-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: MixKD: Towards Efficient Distillation of Large-scale Language Models
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale language models have recently demonstrated impressive empirical performance. Nevertheless, the improved results are attained at the price of bigger models, more power consumption, and slower inference, which hinder their applicability to low-resource (both memory and computation) platforms. Knowledge distillation (KD) has been demonstrated as an effective framework for compressing such big models. However, large-scale neural network systems are prone to memorize training instances, and thus tend to make inconsistent predictions when the data distribution is altered slightly. Moreover, the student model has few opportunities to request useful information from the teacher model when there is limited task-specific data available. To address these issues, we propose MixKD, a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation approach, to endow the resulting model with stronger generalization ability. Concretely, in addition to the original training examples, the student model is encouraged to mimic the teacher's behavior on the linear interpolation of example pairs as well. We prove from a theoretical perspective that under reasonable conditions MixKD gives rise to a smaller gap between the generalization error and the empirical error. To verify its effectiveness, we conduct experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where MixKD consistently leads to significant gains over the standard KD training, and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments under a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Representation-aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a toolbox—combining soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, attention- or layer-aware mappings, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-conscious strategies—KD yields compact models that better preserve teacher behavior while meeting deployment constraints. However, realizing those benefits requires attention to teacher–student compatibility, choice of distilled signals, and data constraints; KD is powerful but not a universal remedy.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL'}]

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a System-Level Primitive for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most effective when treated not as a single loss term but as a system-level design primitive that is matched to data availability, deployment constraints, and student–teacher mismatch. When designers select what to transfer (soft logits, intermediate features, or relational signals), how to expose the student to informative inputs (real, synthesized, or online peer predictions), and how to adapt protocols for distributed or privacy-sensitive settings, KD yields large practical gains in latency, memory, and deployability while controlling risks such as bias transfer or robustness loss. A deployment-aware KD practice leverages representation-aware objectives, data-free synthesis when training data are unavailable, adversarial or online schemes for richer alignment, and federated-distillation architectures for communication-efficient collaboration.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Strategies, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central, pragmatic technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. When applied deliberately — choosing what form of knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle data and deployment constraints — KD routinely yields favorable tradeoffs between model compactness and retained performance. However, distillation is not automatic: data availability, teacher–student mismatches, and application-specific constraints (latency, privacy, heterogeneity) shape both achievable gains and failure modes. Best practice therefore combines representation-aware objectives, curriculum or annealing schedules, multi-teacher or ensemble guidance where helpful, and deployment-aware mechanisms such as data-free generation or privacy-preserving aggregation to realize robust, efficient students.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context-Dependent Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. It delivers meaningful trade-offs between model size, latency, and retained performance when paired with appropriate distillation targets, student-aware design, and complementary compression techniques. However, KD’s success is conditional: it depends on teacher-student capacity alignment, data availability (including privacy constraints), the choice of distilled signals (soft targets versus intermediate features), and optimization practices. Best outcomes arise from task-aware distillation pipelines that combine soft-target transfer, representation-level supervision, and pragmatic strategies such as data synthesis, augmentation, or architecture-aware adjustments.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Pena
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a System-level Primitive for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, versatile approach for shrinking large models into compact students that are deployable under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. Its success depends on treating distillation not as a single loss but as a system design choice: selecting what signals to transfer (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relations), how to align teacher and student architectures and capacities, what data or synthetic surrogates to use, and which complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) to combine. KD delivers substantial efficiency gains in many settings but is context-dependent: careful choices about teacher quality, data availability, and objective design are required to avoid failure modes such as capacity mismatch, degraded handling of low-frequency phenomena, or privacy/robustness tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. KD has been applied successfully to compress large language models, vision transformers, and task-specific architectures, and adapted to settings including self-supervision, multi-task learning, and privacy-sensitive or data-limited regimes. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on the alignment between teacher and student architectures, the availability and quality of data (or of synthetic surrogates), the selection of what knowledge to transfer (logits, features, attention, relational signals), and task-specific choices such as layer-wise matching and curriculum. Recognizing both the demonstrated strengths and the practical failure modes of KD leads to targeted best practices: choose distillation targets that match the student capacity and task, use task-aware or feature-focused objectives for intermediate representations, apply adversarial or synthetic data approaches when original data are unavailable, and explicitly evaluate KD under realistic heterogeneity (e.g., federated or multi-task) to avoid hidden degradations.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and pragmatic framework for compressing large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or more private models across modalities and tasks. When applied thoughtfully — by matching outputs, intermediate representations, training dynamics, or ensembles — KD can preserve or even improve task performance while enabling low-latency inference, reduced memory/compute, and new deployment modes (e.g., federated, data-free, or low-precision). However, distillation is not automatic: design choices about what to transfer, when to transfer, and how to align teacher and student matter for robustness, domain shifts, and rare-token behavior. I argue that best practice combines representation-aware objectives, selective or collaborative teaching strategies, and deployment-aware constraints (privacy, communication, numeric precision) to realize the full benefits of distillation in NLP and other deep learning settings.

papers_seen.author: Cruz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as a primary, practical strategy for compressing large deep models into small, deployable students across vision and language tasks. KD is flexible: it supports soft-target transfer, intermediate representation matching, attention-guided feature matching, multi-teacher ensembles, and data-aware or data-free workflows. When combined with architecture-aware design, low-precision numerics, and data synthesis or augmentation, KD produces compact models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. However, effective deployment requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate risks such as transferred biases, robustness loss, and teacher–student mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Lambert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Contextual Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical toolkit for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the original model's utility. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, and generation tasks show that carefully designed distillation—ranging from soft-target matching to intermediate feature and relational transfer, online co-training, and progressive module replacement—enables large reductions in latency and memory with modest accuracy loss. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability and augmentation, and targeted mitigation of risks such as bias transfer, rare-token degradation, and privacy leakage. Treating KD as a system-level primitive and combining it with complementary compression and data strategies yields the best practical outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Keith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques provide practical pathways to convert large, high-performing models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. Empirically, KD can transfer predictive behavior and internal representations to students that retain much of the teacher’s effectiveness, especially when combined with complementary strategies such as pre-training of compact architectures, careful layer or module mapping, and data-management methods. Successful pipelines trade off accuracy, latency, and model size while navigating constraints such as limited or private data and domain shift. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness (including rare-token behavior), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and developing principled data-free or privacy-preserving distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: May
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target (logit) transfer into a broad toolkit that also includes intermediate representation matching, attention- and layer-aware objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combinations with structural compression. Practical deployments of KD require careful choices about which signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, and how to handle limited or no access to original training data. While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss in many settings, open problems remain in robustness under distribution shift, privacy- and data-constrained regimes, and principled selection of distilled signals for downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Outcomes
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses high-capacity models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Approaches vary from matching final soft targets to transferring intermediate representations, leveraging ensembles or multiple teachers, to data-free synthesis and combining KD with pruning or low-precision numerics. In NLP, KD has enabled compact models to approach the performance of large pre-trained models while substantially reducing inference cost. Recent work clarifies theoretical mechanisms, proposes many-to-many layer alignment techniques, and develops adaptive multi-teacher weighting and zero-shot distillation to broaden applicability. Despite strong empirical gains, open challenges remain in task-specific alignment, robustness to heterogeneous data, and preserving fairness and calibration during compression.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Effective Practices for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques reliably reduce large pretrained models to compact, efficient students suitable for deployment while preserving most of the teacher performance. Across NLP and multimodal tasks, practical compression requires strategies that (1) align representations at multiple levels, (2) focus on task-relevant information, and (3) handle limited or no access to original training data. Combining architecture-aware search, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer selection, and improved input-side strategies (including data augmentation or data-free sample generation) yields compact models with strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs suitable for real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Estes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Across NLP, speech, vision, and recommendation systems, KD reduces inference cost and memory, enables deployment on constrained devices, and can transfer specialized capabilities when paired with appropriate data and training choices. Its effectiveness depends on what is distilled (soft targets, intermediate features, relational signals), the availability and synthesis of training data, and teacher–student design; complementary compression tools and safeguards addressing bias, privacy, and distributional mismatch are often required for robust, real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A diverse set of KD mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate-feature alignment, attention- and relation-based signals, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data synthesis—has been developed and combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance in many vision and language tasks, while remaining sensitive to teacher–student compatibility, data availability, domain shift, and robustness concerns. Practical pipelines therefore co-design student architectures, distillation targets, and data handling strategies to achieve the best trade-offs for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Principled Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' predictive power. KD is most effective when it goes beyond naïve soft-label copying: matching internal representations, aligning inputs and tokenization, choosing appropriate data or synthesis strategies, and adapting teacher updates or curricula all materially affect transfer quality. KD should be used as part of a broader compression pipeline (architecture design, quantization, pruning, or data strategies) and with explicit checks for rare-token behavior, fairness, and robustness. When applied with these considerations, KD reliably produces compact models suitable for production constraints in vision, language, and other modalities.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, more efficient students that retain much of the teacher's performance. Across NLP, vision, and generative models, KD takes many forms (soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention alignment, progressive module replacement, multi-teacher schemes, and data-free synthesis) and is often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost while preserving accuracy under many conditions, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher–student compatibility, the choice of distilled signals, data availability, and optimization protocols. Practical deployment requires careful design choices and remains an active area for research on robustness, rare-token preservation, privacy, and automated student design.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of techniques for transferring knowledge from large teacher models or ensembles into smaller, efficient student models. KD methods span soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-representation and attention alignment, multi-teacher or online schemes, and data- or privacy-aware variants; they are frequently combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical results across vision, speech, language, generative, and 3D tasks show that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation signals, teacher–student alignment, and data strategies are chosen appropriately, but open problems remain around data-free scenarios, robustness to distribution shift, fairness, and automated student design.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become practical tools to reduce model size and computation while retaining much of the performance of large teachers. Across vision, speech, and natural language tasks, approaches include transferring soft logits, mimicking internal features or attention maps, layering/structural adaptations, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-preserving methods. Empirical results demonstrate that careful distillation can yield compact students that approach teacher accuracy and enable deployment in resource-constrained settings, but open challenges remain in robustness, task-specific distillation design, and distributed training dynamics.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a single-teacher trick into a versatile family of methods that enable deployable, compact models across vision and language tasks. Empirical work across domains shows that distillation benefits from adopting strategies that reflect (1) where the student starts (pre-training), (2) what signals it receives (single, multi- or ensemble teachers; feature- and layer-level targets), and (3) the constraints of the deployment context (limited or no access to real data, heterogenous devices, or federated settings). Combining these insights yields practical recipes that reliably close the gap between large models and resource-constrained students while preserving robustness and task performance.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Crosby
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students that retain much of the teacher’s performance. KD spans soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, layer-aware alignment, self-distillation, and architecture-replacement strategies. When combined with appropriate pre-training, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture changes), KD enables practical tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, and memory for NLP and other modalities. Effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, what form of knowledge is transferred, and constraints such as data availability, privacy, fairness, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context-Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of methods for transferring behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller student models, enabling deployment under resource constraints. Rather than a single algorithm, KD comprises multiple signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational losses) and training regimes (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free) that should be chosen to match student capacity, data availability, and downstream requirements. Effective compression usually combines KD with complementary techniques (pretraining, pruning, quantization) and careful alignment between teacher and student. Practical success thus depends on design choices and trade-offs rather than a universal distillation recipe.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.
