papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models by transferring information from high-capacity teachers to smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost and memory while retaining much of the teacher performance. Over the past decade KD has expanded from logits-based soft-target matching to a rich family of techniques including feature- and attention-level alignment, relational and representation matching, student-aware teacher design, and integration with architecture search and other compression primitives. Empirical work across vision and language shows KD both as a route to practical deployment of pre-trained transformers and as a general regularizer that can improve student generalization; ongoing challenges include aligning heterogeneous architectures, coping with limited or private data, and preserving performance on rare classes or tokens. This article synthesizes core methods, mechanistic explanations, practical adaptations for NLP, and directions where KD currently has the greatest impact.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their predictive power. Across vision, language, and generative settings, KD extends from simple softened-logit matching to richer objectives that mimic intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure; it also supports varied training regimes including offline teacher–student, online co-training, multi-teacher curricula, and data-free synthesis. When combined with complementary methods (pretraining, architecture search, pruning, quantization, and federated procedures), KD helps meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints in real deployments. However, success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align architectures, how to handle limited or absent data, and how to avoid transferring undesirable teacher behaviors—issues that remain active research directions.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Multifaceted, and Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical mechanism for turning large, expensive models into smaller, deployable ones while often preserving much of their predictive quality. KD serves multiple roles beyond pure compression — it regularizes learning, enables domain adaptation, supports heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive deployments, and can be adapted at the logit, feature, or data level. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the form of transferred knowledge, data properties (including low-frequency phenomena), and deployment constraints; KD is therefore a powerful but not universally sufficient tool. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a design paradigm with principled choices (what to transfer, how to adapt teachers, how to combine data and synthetic targets, and how to handle heterogeneity) rather than a one-size-fits-all recipe, and it outlines practical recommendations for applying KD across vision and NLP settings.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A diverse set of KD mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate-feature alignment, attention- and relation-based signals, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data synthesis—has been developed and combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance in many vision and language tasks, while remaining sensitive to teacher–student compatibility, data availability, domain shift, and robustness concerns. Practical pipelines therefore co-design student architectures, distillation targets, and data handling strategies to achieve the best trade-offs for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment in constrained environments. Advances across task-adaptive compression, data-free and zero-shot distillation, multi-teacher and meta-learned teaching, and self-distillation demonstrate KD's broad applicability. However, KD is not a panacea: success depends on data availability, the teacher–student optimization dynamics, and explicit design choices around architecture and training signals. Combining pre-training of compact models, task-aware architecture search, and sophisticated distillation protocols yields the best trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Challenges, and Empirical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Approaches extend beyond matching soft logits to include intermediate-feature mimicry, attention-driven layer alignment, many-to-many layer mapping, contrastive representation alignment, and task- or domain-aware search and adaptation. Empirical work shows KD is effective across modalities and tasks — from pre-trained language models and visual-linguistic systems to object detectors, recommender rankers, graph networks, and continual learning settings — but practical deployment requires addressing representation misalignment, task specificity, and catastrophic forgetting. This review synthesizes core strategies and key empirical findings to guide application and future research.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central Tool for Practical Model Compression, with Limits and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. When combined with complementary strategies—such as intermediate-feature alignment, architecture-aware design, data-aware selection, and data-free synthesis—distillation enables practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and resource constraints. However, KD is not universally sufficient: careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data or domain mismatch is required to avoid propagating errors or losing robustness.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Toward Representation- and Strategy-driven Knowledge Distillation for Efficient and Robust NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation remains a central approach to compress large deep learning models for deployment in resource-constrained and domain-specific NLP settings. I argue that to realize reliably compact and generalizable student models we must move past sole reliance on teacher soft-labels and adopt representation-aware objectives, structured channel/feature matching, adaptive training curricula, and practical strategies for low-precision, data-limited, and privacy-sensitive scenarios. Combining these approaches yields students that better capture teacher knowledge, adapt to new domains, and meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Fletcher
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a multifaceted set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger ‘‘teacher’’ models to smaller ‘‘student’’ models to reduce compute, memory, and latency while preserving predictive performance. KD encompasses soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature matching, relational or attention-level supervision, multi-teacher and ensemble compression, and data-centered strategies including augmentation and data-free synthesis. When combined with architecture-aware design, pretraining, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization), KD enables practical deployment across vision, language, graph, and edge settings. However, its success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability and quality, optimization dynamics, and practical concerns such as privacy, robustness, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Trends
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for reducing model size and inference cost while preserving or even improving generalization. The field combines a variety of approaches — from logit-level transfer to feature- and attention-level imitation, from data-free synthesis to multi-teacher ensembles and task-adaptive architecture search — and is applied across domains including NLP, vision, speech and healthcare. Contemporary work integrates distillation with pruning, neural architecture search, federated and privacy-preserving training, and meta-learning for better teacher-student alignment. Empirical results show substantial compression and speedups with modest accuracy loss when distillation is combined with architecture-aware optimization and data- or task-aware strategies. Ongoing challenges include handling imperfect teachers, distribution shift of synthetic data, privacy constraints, and transferring inductive biases across heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Rationale, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical, broadly applicable pathway to compress large neural models into smaller students that retain much of teacher performance. As a flexible toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD supports a range of transfer signals (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention and relational signals), and it integrates naturally with complementary compression mechanisms (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and deployment constraints (latency, privacy, heterogeneity). KD delivers strong empirical gains across modalities and tasks when matched to student capacity and data conditions, but it is not a universal fix: success requires careful teacher–student design, data and curriculum strategies, and safeguards for distribution shift and rare-token fidelity. The position taken here is that KD should be treated as a first‑line, default strategy for model compression in deep learning and NLP—used proactively and in combination with other compression primitives—while acknowledging its failure modes and design requirements.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Evidence for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) enables deployment of high-performing but large neural models by training compact student models that mimic larger teachers. Empirical work across speech, NLP, vision, and federated settings shows KD reduces model size and inference cost while preserving accuracy, and its effectiveness increases when combined with complementary techniques: pre-training compact architectures, adaptive layer mapping for transformers, data-centric augmentations, ensemble teachers, and robustness-aware objectives. This paper synthesizes results from recent studies to argue that a principled KD pipeline—pre-train compact students, match representations flexibly, leverage data augmentation and teacher ensembles, and incorporate robustness or task-specific objectives—yields the best tradeoff between efficiency and performance for practical deployments.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Failure Modes, and Practical Recipes
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, recommendation, and NLP. KD techniques range from simple logits matching to representation-level transfer, multi-teacher schemes, adversarial sample synthesis, and progressive module replacement. While many distillation recipes recover most of a teacher’s accuracy and enable large efficiency gains, the success of KD depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle limited or absent training data. Careful design—matching distillation targets to student capacity, mitigating transferred errors, and combining distillation with complementary compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search)—yields robust, efficient models for practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. KD has been applied successfully to compress large language models, vision transformers, and task-specific architectures, and adapted to settings including self-supervision, multi-task learning, and privacy-sensitive or data-limited regimes. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on the alignment between teacher and student architectures, the availability and quality of data (or of synthetic surrogates), the selection of what knowledge to transfer (logits, features, attention, relational signals), and task-specific choices such as layer-wise matching and curriculum. Recognizing both the demonstrated strengths and the practical failure modes of KD leads to targeted best practices: choose distillation targets that match the student capacity and task, use task-aware or feature-focused objectives for intermediate representations, apply adversarial or synthetic data approaches when original data are unavailable, and explicitly evaluate KD under realistic heterogeneity (e.g., federated or multi-task) to avoid hidden degradations.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Open Questions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses techniques that transfer information from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students). Across computer vision and natural language tasks, KD has been applied as logit-level supervision, feature mimicking, ensemble compression, self-distillation, domain-adaptive compression, and data-free/privacypreserving variants. Empirical work shows that distilled students can approach teacher performance while improving latency and footprint, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data complexity, and whether distillation occurs at the logits or feature level. Recent analyses link KD to label smoothing and show promising teacher-free or self-distillation approaches, while practical applications demonstrate domain-specific adaptation, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, and techniques to mitigate degenerate behaviours in sequence generation. Remaining challenges include handling domain shift, preserving low-frequency lexical details, training without original data, and principled teacher selection.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones that are deployable in resource-constrained settings. A rich set of distillation strategies has been developed: matching teacher output distributions, transferring intermediate representations, adversarial or data-free synthesis of training examples, multi-teacher aggregation, and contrastive or projector-based representation alignment. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance in many tasks (including NLP and graph learning), but practical success depends strongly on optimization details, the availability and alignment of data, and careful design of the distillation objective. Privacy-preserving variants and methods tailored to domain-specific architectures (e.g., GNNs, transformers) extend KD’s applicability, while also introducing trade-offs between utility, robustness, and guarantees. This synthesis summarizes key methods, empirical findings, and known limitations to guide research and practice in KD for deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Donovan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential and Practical, but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD can preserve much of a teacher's performance while reducing parameter count and inference cost, but its reliability depends on choices about what to distill, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited, heterogeneous, or private data. Realistic deployment requires combining KD with complementary compression techniques, adapting the distillation signal to the task and student capacity, and evaluating robustness and privacy implications.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer information from larger, often over-parameterized teacher models into smaller, more efficient students to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD strategies vary in what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate representations, relations), how it is transferred (logit matching, feature-mimicking, projector layers, contrastive objectives, adversarial losses), and in deployment settings (data-available, data-free, federated or distributed, and online). Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, distilled students frequently recover much of teacher performance while enabling practical gains in speed and memory; however, method choice, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and distributional shifts materially affect outcomes, and open problems remain in preserving rare-token behavior, transferring robustness and fairness, and compressing across heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Turner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable method for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When combined with complementary practices—such as pretraining compact students, representation-level matching, curriculum scheduling, teacher ensembles, and data augmentation—KD yields strong tradeoffs between efficiency and performance across modalities and tasks. However, its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data or domain mismatch; KD therefore functions best as a central, flexible component within a broader compression pipeline rather than as a one-size-fits-all cure.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, System-Level Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact student models that preserve much of a larger teacher’s accuracy while meeting latency, memory, and deployment constraints. KD succeeds most reliably when treated as a system-level design choice rather than a single auxiliary loss: practitioners should choose what signals to transfer (logits, features, attention, relations), align student and teacher architectures, incorporate complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and address data limitations through augmentation or data-free/federated strategies. KD has proven value across modalities but also carries risks — optimization difficulties, teacher errors propagated to students, and sensitivity to available data — that require explicit mitigation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information from teacher models. KD encompasses a family of techniques — matching teacher logits (soft targets), aligning intermediate features or attention maps, online or mutual distillation, self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware variants — that are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance in vision and language tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality and specialization, student capacity and architecture, availability and alignment of data, and optimization choices; naive distillation can propagate teacher errors or fail under strong teacher–student mismatch. Practical pipelines therefore select distillation signals and schedules appropriate to task and deployment constraints, often pairing KD with complementary compression techniques to trade compute and size for modest predictive degradation.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted set of techniques for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students that retain much of the teachers' performance. Modern KD extends beyond soft-label matching to include representation-level objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, data-free or zero-shot variants, and architecture-aware combinations with pruning, quantization, and search. KD has been applied successfully across domains — including language generation, ranking, detection, and federated settings — but its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to manage data, privacy, and distributional shift. Practical deployment requires selecting distillation signals and training regimes that match student capacity and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: The Pragmatic Power and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured into a practical toolkit for shrinking models, transferring behavior across architectures and modalities, and enabling deployment under compute, memory, or privacy constraints. Beyond straightforward teacher-to-student compression, distillation techniques combine with data augmentation, synthetic-data generation, and regularization to address limited data, cross-domain gaps, and interpretability needs. However, outcomes depend on choices about teacher quality, training data availability, and objective design; careful method selection is required to realize reliable, production-ready gains.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. Over the past decade a diverse family of distillation methods has emerged—logit-level soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, data-free or zero-shot synthesis, multi-teacher ensembles, and privacy-aware adaptations—applied across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative models. Practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data availability and domain mismatch; combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, architecture search, quantization) and task-aware pipelines yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated framework that enables transferring predictive power from large, expensive models to smaller, deployable ones. KD supports diverse practical constraints — absent training data, limited downstream-task data, domain shifts, multi-task settings, and architectural mismatches — and couples naturally with automated model search and targeted feature imitation. By viewing KD as a family of techniques (logit transfer, feature mimicking, adversarial-sample guidance, synthetic-data distillation, and teacher-ensemble strategies) practitioners can compress models while retaining or even improving task-relevant inductive structure and generalization.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches and Insights in Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer useful information from larger, more expensive models (or ensembles) to smaller, deployable models. Research spans theoretical analyses of what is transferred, architectural and loss-design strategies to improve feature and output matching, specialized teacher–student training regimes (including multi-teacher and student-aware teacher training), online and federated distillation for large-scale or privacy-sensitive settings, and structural compression strategies that preserve accuracy while reducing memory and compute. Applications include image models, generative models, question-answering systems and multi-task natural language understanding, with methods tailored to domain constraints such as heterogeneous device capabilities and privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Multi-purpose Strategy for Model Compression and Robust Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD supports domain adaptation, latency-aware architecture transformations, robustness transfer, and interpretable model surrogates. When combined with careful training protocols (e.g., multi-teacher schemes, domain adaptation, or targeted regularization), distillation enables deployment of high-performing models in resource- and latency-constrained or safety-critical settings across vision, speech, 3D perception, and natural language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Theory, and Practical Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted approach to compress large deep models and transfer knowledge to smaller, faster, or more interpretable models. Across vision and language applications, KD encompasses teacher-student paradigms that use teacher soft targets, intermediate representations, or auxiliary objectives; extensions include multi-teacher setups, data-free distillation, meta-learned teachers, and device-aware distillation for heterogeneous deployments. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of the teacher performance while enabling orders-of-magnitude reductions in parameters and inference cost; theoretical and empirical analyses clarify when and why distillation helps and how dataset complexity, teacher quality, and student capacity interact to determine outcomes. Practical strategies combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware techniques to meet deployment constraints while retaining generalization.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods have become central tools for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy and capabilities of large teachers. Research over the past decade has produced a diverse set of techniques—ranging from distilling logits, internal representations, and attention patterns to data-free and few-shot strategies, multi-teacher ensembles, and task-adaptive search for student architectures. These approaches have been applied across vision, language, multimodal, and deployed/distributed settings, demonstrating substantial gains in inference speed and model size while exposing trade-offs in robustness, data requirements, and modality alignment. This survey summarizes the main algorithmic families, common engineering strategies, notable empirical outcomes, and key open challenges for applying distillation in practice.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques provide a set of complementary strategies to transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller student models. Methods span matching output distributions (soft targets), imitating intermediate representations and attention, aligning layers, using multiple teachers or self-teaching schedules, and applying task- or data-aware procedures including data-free generation and low-precision adaptation. Empirical work shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance while gaining speed and memory efficiency, but outcomes depend on which knowledge is transferred, student capacity, data availability, and task specificity. Practical deployments combine distillation with architecture search, quantization, and curriculum or augmentation strategies to balance fidelity, robustness, and resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Capabilities, Mechanisms, and Constraints
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, efficient students suitable for production. KD methods span soft-label transfer, representation- and layer-level matching, adversarial and privacy-aware variants, and meta- or teacher-adaptive strategies. When combined with appropriate pre-training, architecture-aware adapters, and task-aware objectives, distillation yields compact models that approach teacher performance under realistic compute, data, and deployment constraints. However, outcomes depend on teacher–student compatibility, what signals are distilled, and whether robustness or privacy guarantees are required.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Tran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques transfer behaviors of large models into smaller, more efficient models by supervising students with information derived from teachers (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention, or synthetic labels). Empirical results across vision, speech, and language show that carefully designed distillation pipelines can preserve much of a teacher’s performance while reducing size and latency. Effective practice combines choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data strategies (including augmentation or synthesis), and complementary structural compression. Remaining challenges include handling imperfect teachers, limited or private data, robustness and out-of-distribution behavior, and principled automation of trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Mckee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and distributed settings KD often recovers much of a teacher's predictive performance while enabling faster inference, lower memory use, and deployment under resource or privacy constraints. However, KD is not a panacea: outcomes depend on what signals are transferred (logits, features, attention), teacher–student compatibility, availability and quality of data (including data-free or federated setups), and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Best practice treats distillation as one element of a compression pipeline that combines representation matching, architecture-aware student design, data strategies, and risk-aware training protocols.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models so that students retain much of the teachers' task performance while reducing inference cost and resource consumption. The practice extends beyond matching final logits to include feature- and layer-level supervision, attention- or projector-based alignment, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware strategies (including data-free or synthetic-data approaches). KD has been applied across modalities and deployment regimes (on-device, privacy-aware, and distributed/federated settings), and empirical work highlights both practical successes and recurring failure modes such as sensitivity to teacher-student mismatch, domain shift, and preservation of rare or low-frequency signals. Current best practices emphasize combining representation-level objectives, careful input/data handling, and co-design of teacher and student; open problems remain around robustness, heterogeneity, and automated student design.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression approaches seek to transfer useful information from larger, often over-parameterized teacher models into smaller, deployable student models while preserving performance. Research has expanded beyond matching final logits to include feature- and layer-level supervision, adaptive layer alignments, many-to-many mappings, task-aware filtering, teacher-free alternatives, data- and communication-constrained settings, and careful use of input-side techniques such as data augmentation. Empirical work shows these strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher accuracy across vision and language tasks, and practical pipelines combine pre-training of compact architectures with targeted distillation to improve downstream performance and deployment efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a simple teacher-student training recipe into a multifaceted toolkit that enables efficient, robust, and privacy-aware deployment of deep models. KD not only compresses large models into faster, smaller students suitable for edge and production, but also enables task-adaptive compression, data-limited or data-free scenarios, privacy-preserving federated setups, and transfers of inductive biases across architectures. When combined with complementary techniques such as architecture search, specialized feature-matching losses, and careful input-side interventions, KD yields practical compressed models without prohibitive losses in accuracy and can improve generalization in out-of-distribution settings.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques train compact student models to emulate larger teachers, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints across vision, speech, and language tasks. The body of work spans logits- or soft-target matching, feature- and layer-wise representation transfer, architecture-aware transformations, data-free and privacy-preserving methods, and multi-teacher or progressive schemes. Empirical and theoretical studies together show KD often improves student generalization and enables substantial efficiency gains, but outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution, and optimization choices. Practical pipelines combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search while addressing failure modes such as teacher errors, low-frequency token degradation, and domain shifts.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First-line, Context-aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with attention to what knowledge is transferred, how intermediate layers are aligned, and whether data or privacy constraints hold, KD can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance while enabling large gains in inference speed and memory. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: optimization difficulties, mismatches in capacity between teacher and student, and limited or private data require tailored objectives, architecture-aware choices, and complementary techniques. This essay argues KD should be a primary strategy in model-compression toolkits while recommending concrete practices to increase reliability across real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. It generalizes from soft-target supervision to intermediate-representation matching, multi-teacher ensembles, and data-free synthesis. When combined with complementary strategies (pre-training of compact models, data augmentation, pruning, and hardware-aware layout), KD enables substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while largely preserving task performance. Realizing these gains requires careful choices about what knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to handle limited or sensitive data; when these are addressed, KD serves as a reliable foundation for practical compression pipelines in NLP and other domains.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Efficient Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a foundational technique for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy of larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and graph domains. When applied thoughtfully — combining representational objectives, teacher-student co-design, task-aware compression, and appropriate data strategies — KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices while maintaining robustness and fairness. However, pitfalls arise from mismatches in inputs, teacher strength, data availability, and dataset biases; practical KD should therefore be integrated with complementary methods (e.g., architecture search, pruning, curriculum strategies, and data-generation) and with safeguards for ethical concerns.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. KD operates through complementary mechanisms — soft-target regularization, internal representation transfer, and architecture- or data-aware adaptations — and integrates naturally with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design). When applied with attention to teacher quality, signal selection (logits vs features), and data constraints, distillation produces efficient models that are usable in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained deployments. However, KD has systematic limitations tied to teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, and potential transfer of undesirable behaviors, which motivate principled combinations of KD recipes and deployment-aware practices.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.
