papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, efficient students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. A broad family of KD techniques has been developed—matching softened logits, aligning intermediate representations or attention, using multi-teacher or online co-training schedules, and synthesizing or augmenting data for training students. KD often recovers much of a teacher's performance while reducing parameter count and inference cost, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data alignment, and training dynamics. Practical deployments combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, progressive module replacement) and must address open challenges including heterogeneous or federated settings, data scarcity or privacy constraints, robustness under distribution shift, and preservation of low-frequency or domain-specific signals.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Multifaceted, and Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical mechanism for turning large, expensive models into smaller, deployable ones while often preserving much of their predictive quality. KD serves multiple roles beyond pure compression — it regularizes learning, enables domain adaptation, supports heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive deployments, and can be adapted at the logit, feature, or data level. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the form of transferred knowledge, data properties (including low-frequency phenomena), and deployment constraints; KD is therefore a powerful but not universally sufficient tool. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a design paradigm with principled choices (what to transfer, how to adapt teachers, how to combine data and synthetic targets, and how to handle heterogeneity) rather than a one-size-fits-all recipe, and it outlines practical recommendations for applying KD across vision and NLP settings.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become the primary, practical method for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. KD unifies multiple training strategies—soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, multi-teacher schedules, and data-free synthesis—enabling substantial reductions in inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. In practice, KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search) and when its objectives and data regimes are chosen to match student capacity and deployment constraints. Despite its strengths, KD has known weaknesses, including sensitivity to teacher–student mismatch, degradation under data heterogeneity, and risks of transferring undesirable behaviors; addressing these requires careful protocol design, selective transfer of teacher signals, and hybrid pipelines that integrate KD with data-centric and architecture-centric interventions.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression — Powerful but Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large deep learning and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. KD provides flexible supervision signals (soft targets, intermediate features, attention patterns) that enable substantial reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability, and task specificity. Realistic deployment therefore requires combining KD with complementary strategies (task-aware layer selection, architecture search, data augmentation or synthesis, multi-teacher schemes, and privacy-aware mechanisms) and evaluating tradeoffs under the target constraints.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: Principled Use of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, practical method for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while retaining much of teacher performance. However, its success is conditional: choices about what to transfer, how to supervise internal representations, how to design student architectures for particular tasks, and how to handle data, distribution shift, and fairness constraints materially affect outcomes. I argue that KD should be treated as a flexible design pattern—combining soft-target transfer, internal-representation matching, task-adaptive architecture design, and explicit fairness or data strategies—to produce reliable, deployable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Wise
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Methods, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. By transferring richer supervision than hard labels—soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or aggregated multi-teacher signals—KD enables compact models that retain much of teacher performance while supporting complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware changes). KD also adapts to constrained settings (limited or private data, domain-specialization, federated or black-box teachers) but requires careful design choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and training curricula. When applied as part of a principled compression pipeline, KD offers a practical route to deployable high-quality models, though open problems remain in preserving rare-token behaviors, robustness, and reliable operation under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and selected internal information from teacher models. KD methods range from matching softened teacher logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure, and are commonly combined with complementary engineering strategies (architecture design, pretraining of compact models, quantization, and data augmentation). Empirical evidence shows distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision and language tasks while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability and augmentation, and the relative strength and role of the teacher; these choices shape practical tradeoffs in robustness, fairness, and cross-distribution generalization.

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Foundation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD spans logit-level supervision, intermediate-feature matching, progressive architecture replacement, adversarial and data-free variants, and combinations with structural compression and pruning. When applied with attention to the distilled signal, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and optimization protocol, KD reliably reduces memory, latency, and compute costs across vision, language, generative, and graph domains. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on careful method selection, complementary compression steps, and mitigation of teacher–student mismatch and data limitations.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Findings, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring useful predictive behavior or internal structure from one or more teachers. A rich set of KD approaches exists — from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate representation imitation, attention and feature alignment, adversarial and projector-based techniques, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or federated variants — and these have been applied across NLP, vision, graph-structured data, multimodal models, and generative models. Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, but its success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher/student compatibility, data availability, and task-specific constraints. Important practical concerns include preserving rare-token behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher errors or biases, enabling privacy-preserving or data-free compression, and combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Unifying Tool: Compression, Transfer, and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) began as a model compression technique but has evolved into a flexible framework that accomplishes compression, regularization, domain adaptation, continual learning, fairness mitigation, and inductive-bias transfer across architectures and modalities. By choosing what to transfer (logits, features, relations, or module behavior) and how to weight multi-source supervision, practitioners can adapt KD to the constraints and objectives of specific tasks. This paper argues that KD should be treated not merely as a compression trick but as a general-purpose mechanism for shaping student models, and it synthesizes empirical and theoretical evidence to recommend practical best practices for applying KD across modern deep learning and NLP settings.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a heuristic into a central, practical toolkit for compressing large models and transferring behavior from high-capacity teachers into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative modeling, practitioners combine soft-label supervision, intermediate-representation matching, data- and privacy-aware strategies, and architecture-aware choices to trade accuracy for latency, memory, and power. KD is effective when paired with complementary techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, synthetic-data generation, curriculum schedules), but its success depends critically on what form of knowledge is distilled, how data or augmentations are used, and how teacher–student capacity and domain mismatches are managed. Remaining challenges include robust data-free distillation, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, mitigating bias transfer, and firm theoretical characterizations that predict when and how distillation will work in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely applicable strategy for compressing large neural models by transferring information from one or more high-capacity teacher models to smaller student models. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals), how teacher and student are aligned, and the data available for training, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of the original performance. KD also integrates naturally with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adapts to specialized settings such as multi-teacher ensembles, heterogeneous-device deployments, generative-model compression, low-precision inference, and privacy-sensitive or data-limited environments. However, KD is not uniformly automatic: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, student capacity, distributional match, and design of distillation objectives and curricula.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential but Context‑Dependent Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied deliberately—choosing which teacher signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacity and inputs, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques—KD routinely delivers large reductions in model size and latency while preserving most task performance. Real-world success requires representation-aware objectives, options for data-limited or privacy-sensitive settings, and careful evaluation under distribution shift and modality-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models to reproduce useful behavior of larger teacher models so that deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints becomes practical. KD encompasses a family of techniques — from matching teacher output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure — and is commonly combined with complementary compressions such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows that, when matched to student capacity and data availability, distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Practical success depends on choices about which signals to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data access (including data-free alternatives), and robustness or fairness requirements; remaining challenges concern principled objective design, optimization under capacity mismatch, and reliable transfer of robustness and rare-token/long-tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Treated as a toolbox rather than a single loss term, KD delivers meaningful efficiency gains across modalities when the distillation targets, student design, and data strategy are chosen for the deployment constraints. However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis methods, and robustness to distribution shift. Practical success therefore requires combining KD with complementary compression techniques, carefully selecting what to transfer, and evaluating students under realistic deployment conditions.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Theory, and Practical Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted approach to compress large deep models and transfer knowledge to smaller, faster, or more interpretable models. Across vision and language applications, KD encompasses teacher-student paradigms that use teacher soft targets, intermediate representations, or auxiliary objectives; extensions include multi-teacher setups, data-free distillation, meta-learned teachers, and device-aware distillation for heterogeneous deployments. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of the teacher performance while enabling orders-of-magnitude reductions in parameters and inference cost; theoretical and empirical analyses clarify when and why distillation helps and how dataset complexity, teacher quality, and student capacity interact to determine outcomes. Practical strategies combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware techniques to meet deployment constraints while retaining generalization.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Gilbert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers. By transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels—ranging from softened logits to intermediate representations and relational signals—KD enables substantial reductions in parameters and latency while preserving much of the teacher's performance. When combined with complementary compression tools and careful teacher–student co-design, distillation provides a practical first-line strategy for real-world model compression, though important open problems remain around fairness, data availability, heterogeneity, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Compact, Robust, and Adaptable Deep Models in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers while enabling domain adaptation, deployment under resource constraints, privacy-preserving releases, and improved robustness. KD techniques span transfer from full teacher ensembles to single students, intermediate-layer alignment, self-distillation, and even data-free distillation; each variant addresses different operational constraints. However, distillation also carries risks (e.g., transfer of undesirable biases) and requires careful design choices (e.g., what information to transfer and what data to use). Combining advances across these variants yields effective, small NLP models fit for real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Potter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Bounded Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-strategy approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD methods include transferring softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations, progressive module replacement, and data-free or few-shot variants to handle limited or private data. Best results come from treating KD as one element of a broader compression pipeline that also incorporates architecture-aware choices, data strategies, and explicit attention to robustness and fairness. KD is therefore a central tool for efficient deployment, but it has clear limits and must be designed carefully to avoid transferring undesirable behaviors or losing rare-token performance.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers in both vision and natural language tasks. Empirical work shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints, and many variants extend KD beyond soft-target transfer to feature matching, multi-teacher schemes, progressive replacement, and domain-adaptive workflows. At the same time, theoretical and empirical analyses reveal optimization barriers, sensitivity to the choice of data and teacher signals, and imperfect matching between teacher and student as important limits. This review argues that KD is a powerful but context-dependent tool: its success requires matching the distillation signal to student capacity and task complexity, combining KD with complementary compression techniques, and paying careful attention to data and training dynamics to avoid degenerate outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural teachers into smaller student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision and language tasks, KD techniques include soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention- or relation-based alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher fusion, and data- or domain-aware variations. Empirical work shows that distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to meet deployment constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, available data, and training objectives. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, transferring robustness and inductive biases, and handling heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive environments.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Cobb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. KD transfers information beyond hard labels — including softened output distributions, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational signals — and is commonly combined with architectural or numerical compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest performance loss when teacher–student design, data availability, and optimization dynamics are considered; however, its success is contingent on capacity alignment, data choices, and safeguards against transferring undesirable behaviors. Applications range from accelerated inference and edge deployment to domain adaptation, federated learning, and task-specific adaptations such as non-autoregressive translation and graph-to-MLP compression.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Effective Knowledge Distillation for Deployable Deep Models: Evidence, Techniques, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool to compress large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, KD has enabled domain adaptation, model-size reduction, cross-lingual transfer, and deployment under resource constraints. Success depends on (1) aligning teacher and student inputs and intermediate representations, (2) choosing appropriate supervision signals (soft labels, intermediate-feature losses, attention-based guidance), (3) handling the absence of original training data when necessary, and (4) adapting compression to task and domain requirements. This review synthesizes empirical and methodological findings from recent studies to recommend principled KD choices for practitioners aiming to deploy compact, robust models in real-world NLP and related tasks.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students) to reduce inference cost and memory while retaining task performance. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational or structural signals), how teachers and students are aligned (layer mappings, many-to-many correspondences), how data is used (original training data, synthetic or generated data, or no data), and how multiple teachers or online training regimes are incorporated. KD is routinely combined with architectural compression (pruning, quantization, and architecture search) and used across vision, language, graph, and generative-model settings. Empirical and practical work shows KD can produce compact models suitable for deployment, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful design of distillation objectives and training curricula.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for transferring information from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable student models so as to reduce inference cost while preserving predictive performance. KD spans soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, layer-wise alignment, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or zero-shot methods for cases where original training data are unavailable. In practice KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression building blocks (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when design choices account for teacher–student capacity, data availability, and task-specific objectives. Remaining practical challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, preserving fine-grained behaviors (e.g., rare tokens or safety-critical outputs), and principled methods for data-free or privacy-sensitive distillation.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a versatile family of techniques that can preserve performance while enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings, but it must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints. Effective KD requires attention to the teacher-student relationship (including training teachers that are "student-friendly"), to data availability (including data-free approaches), and to distributional mismatches (e.g., federated or heterogeneous-device scenarios). When such concerns are addressed—via task-adaptive compression, feature- or relation-aware transfer, multi-teacher or ensemble signals, or methods that expose raw data signals lost in naive distillation—KD can deliver near-teacher performance at far lower cost. However, KD has known failure modes (such as propagating teacher errors on low-frequency tokens or degrading under data heterogeneity) that demand targeted remedies. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an adaptable design pattern: choose techniques that match your downstream objective (accuracy, latency, privacy, heterogeneity) rather than applying a one-size-fits-all distillation loss.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of model-compression techniques that trains smaller student models to reproduce useful behavior from larger teacher models. Across vision and language tasks, KD methods extend beyond matching soft teacher outputs to include alignment of internal representations, attention or relational signals, adversarially-informed objectives, online or multi-teacher schemes, and data-aware strategies. Effective application balances what is transferred, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and robustness or fairness constraints, and it is typically combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search for deployment in resource-constrained environments.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller students that are deployable under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When applied thoughtfully—choosing what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, relational signals), aligning teacher and student architectures and tokenization, and combining KD with complementary techniques such as architecture search or targeted pruning—distillation routinely yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance and sometimes even improve generalization. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on data availability, teacher quality and friendliness, domain shifts, and the specific form of knowledge chosen for transfer. Effective deployment therefore requires principled design of the distillation objective, curricula or annealing schedules, and safeguards for robustness and rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Responsible Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring useful predictive and representational knowledge from teacher models to students. When combined with complementary techniques (e.g., layer mapping, multi-teacher weighting, data-free synthesis, pruning, and quantization) and guided by student-aware design and fairness/robustness constraints, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of a teacher's accuracy. Practical deployment of KD requires attention to data availability, teacher quality, and domain-specific constraints to avoid propagating undesirable behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. It generalizes from soft-target supervision to intermediate-representation matching, multi-teacher ensembles, and data-free synthesis. When combined with complementary strategies (pre-training of compact models, data augmentation, pruning, and hardware-aware layout), KD enables substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while largely preserving task performance. Realizing these gains requires careful choices about what knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to handle limited or sensitive data; when these are addressed, KD serves as a reliable foundation for practical compression pipelines in NLP and other domains.

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Foundation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD spans logit-level supervision, intermediate-feature matching, progressive architecture replacement, adversarial and data-free variants, and combinations with structural compression and pruning. When applied with attention to the distilled signal, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and optimization protocol, KD reliably reduces memory, latency, and compute costs across vision, language, generative, and graph domains. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on careful method selection, complementary compression steps, and mitigation of teacher–student mismatch and data limitations.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary Compression Strategy for Practical Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the first-line strategy for compressing large deep models into deployable students: it reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal representations, is broadly applicable across modalities, and composes naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD is not a silver bullet — its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data availability, and how knowledge is represented and aligned — so production pipelines should combine KD with representation-aware objectives, student pretraining, and targeted data strategies to mitigate distributional and optimization pitfalls. When applied with these caveats, KD delivers strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs that make large pretrained models practical for constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become practical tools to reduce model size and computation while retaining much of the performance of large teachers. Across vision, speech, and natural language tasks, approaches include transferring soft logits, mimicking internal features or attention maps, layering/structural adaptations, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-preserving methods. Empirical results demonstrate that careful distillation can yield compact students that approach teacher accuracy and enable deployment in resource-constrained settings, but open challenges remain in robustness, task-specific distillation design, and distributed training dynamics.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers knowledge from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost while attempting to preserve predictive performance. KD encompasses a range of mechanisms — soft-target (logit) matching, feature and intermediate-layer imitation, attention- or channel-based guidance, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, self-distillation, and data- or device-aware variants — and is applied across modalities including vision and language. Empirical work shows KD can yield substantial reductions in parameters and latency with modest accuracy loss, and in some settings can improve student generalization. Practical deployment couples KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and requires careful design choices around teacher-student alignment, data availability, and task-specific objectives.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques train compact student models to emulate larger teachers, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints across vision, speech, and language tasks. The body of work spans logits- or soft-target matching, feature- and layer-wise representation transfer, architecture-aware transformations, data-free and privacy-preserving methods, and multi-teacher or progressive schemes. Empirical and theoretical studies together show KD often improves student generalization and enables substantial efficiency gains, but outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution, and optimization choices. Practical pipelines combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search while addressing failure modes such as teacher errors, low-frequency token degradation, and domain shifts.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other forms of teacher knowledge. Across vision and language tasks KD has enabled practical reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on what form of knowledge is transferred, how teacher and student representations are aligned, the availability and selection of data for distillation, and complementary compression techniques such as low-precision numerics, pruning, or architecture adaptation. Remaining challenges include optimization barriers that prevent exact teacher matching, reliable distillation without original data, robustness and fairness under compression, and principled methods for matching heterogeneous teacher–student pairs.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models so that the students retain much of the teachers' performance while meeting resource, latency, or privacy constraints. KD methods include matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate representations or attention, synthesizing surrogate training data when original data are unavailable, and deploying progressive or ensemble-based strategies. Practical pipelines commonly combine KD with architecture-aware compression (pruning, quantization, or search) and training-time strategies (curricula, online distillation, or federated protocols) to balance efficiency and accuracy. Despite strong empirical success across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, open challenges remain in aligning heterogeneous teacher–student architectures, operating under limited or private data, and designing principled objectives and curricula that preserve robustness and task-specific inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic into a practical, multi-purpose toolkit for compressing large models while preserving performance across domains and modalities. KD enables deployment of powerful models on resource-constrained devices, supports domain adaptation, helps preserve privacy, and can be adapted to architectures ranging from transformers to GANs and GNNs. Complementary techniques — e.g., architectural replacement, data augmentation, multi-teacher schemes, and precision reduction — expand KD’s effectiveness. However, KD’s success depends on how knowledge is represented and transferred (logits, internal representations, relations) and on availability or synthesis of appropriate data. The balance of method and setting determines whether KD yields compact models that meet real-world constraints without unacceptable loss of fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. KD has been applied successfully to compress large language models, vision transformers, and task-specific architectures, and adapted to settings including self-supervision, multi-task learning, and privacy-sensitive or data-limited regimes. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on the alignment between teacher and student architectures, the availability and quality of data (or of synthetic surrogates), the selection of what knowledge to transfer (logits, features, attention, relational signals), and task-specific choices such as layer-wise matching and curriculum. Recognizing both the demonstrated strengths and the practical failure modes of KD leads to targeted best practices: choose distillation targets that match the student capacity and task, use task-aware or feature-focused objectives for intermediate representations, apply adversarial or synthetic data approaches when original data are unavailable, and explicitly evaluate KD under realistic heterogeneity (e.g., federated or multi-task) to avoid hidden degradations.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context‑Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a multifaceted approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with attention to which signals are transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention), the teacher–student relationship, data availability, and deployment constraints, KD yields substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher behavior. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on capacity alignment, data and distributional match, and careful objective design. Practical adoption therefore requires selecting KD variants that fit task and system constraints and combining KD with complementary techniques (pretraining, data augmentation, multi-teacher signals, or architecture co-design) to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses information from larger, often more expensive teacher models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. Research over the past decade has developed a spectrum of KD objectives (soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, contrastive and relational losses), training regimes (offline teacher-student, online co-training, self-distillation, multi-teacher schedules), and deployment-aware integrations (pre-training students, architecture-aware adapters, and combination with pruning or quantization). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance while reducing parameter count and latency, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and the choice of what and how to transfer. Ongoing challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, matching heterogeneous architectures, preserving low-frequency or domain-specific signals, and automating trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.
