papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students for deployment in deep learning and NLP. A broad family of KD techniques—ranging from softened-logit supervision to intermediate representation matching, attention- and feature-level imitation, many-to-many layer alignment, adversarial and data-free variants, and task- or device-aware architecture search—enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while often retaining most of the teacher's performance. Effective application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, whether and how to use original data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. Important open problems remain regarding theoretical understanding, robustness under distribution shift or imperfect teachers, and scalable private or data-free distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: May
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target (logit) transfer into a broad toolkit that also includes intermediate representation matching, attention- and layer-aware objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combinations with structural compression. Practical deployments of KD require careful choices about which signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, and how to handle limited or no access to original training data. While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss in many settings, open problems remain in robustness under distribution shift, privacy- and data-constrained regimes, and principled selection of distilled signals for downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. KD operates through complementary mechanisms — soft-target regularization, internal representation transfer, and architecture- or data-aware adaptations — and integrates naturally with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design). When applied with attention to teacher quality, signal selection (logits vs features), and data constraints, distillation produces efficient models that are usable in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained deployments. However, KD has systematic limitations tied to teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, and potential transfer of undesirable behaviors, which motivate principled combinations of KD recipes and deployment-aware practices.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has proven to be a practical and versatile approach for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. KD variants transfer soft targets, intermediate representations, attention patterns, or synthetic data to students, enabling substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. When combined with task-aware design, layer-mapping, multi-teacher schedules, and appropriate input-side strategies, distillation supports robust deployment across NLP and other modalities. Nevertheless, careful design is required to manage teacher–student mismatch, preserve low-frequency or domain-specific signals, and operate when original training data is limited or unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment in constrained environments. Advances across task-adaptive compression, data-free and zero-shot distillation, multi-teacher and meta-learned teaching, and self-distillation demonstrate KD's broad applicability. However, KD is not a panacea: success depends on data availability, the teacher–student optimization dynamics, and explicit design choices around architecture and training signals. Combining pre-training of compact models, task-aware architecture search, and sophisticated distillation protocols yields the best trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Estes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Across NLP, speech, vision, and recommendation systems, KD reduces inference cost and memory, enables deployment on constrained devices, and can transfer specialized capabilities when paired with appropriate data and training choices. Its effectiveness depends on what is distilled (soft targets, intermediate features, relational signals), the availability and synthesis of training data, and teacher–student design; complementary compression tools and safeguards addressing bias, privacy, and distributional mismatch are often required for robust, real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their accuracy and desirable properties. Methods differ in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure) and in how and when the transfer occurs (offline teacher-to-student, online/co-distillation, adversarial/ensemble-driven, or data-free with synthetic samples). Across vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks, KD is routinely combined with architecture-aware choices and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, and domain-adaptation constraints. Empirical work shows strong gains in efficiency, but also highlights limitations: dependence on teacher quality and data alignment, possible degradation under domain shift or when sensitive attributes are transferred, and open problems in data-free or privacy-preserving settings. This synthesis summarizes key mechanisms, representative variants, cross-modal applications, common engineering practices, and the principal open challenges informed by recent empirical and survey literature.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are a widely adopted toolkit for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy of larger teachers. Research across vision and language characterizes KD as a family of methods—transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, relational structure, or training signals via specialized curricula or online exchanges—and shows that KD integrates naturally with pretraining, architecture design, and deployment-aware strategies. Practical success depends on matching the choice of knowledge (what to transfer), the teacher-student pairing (capacity and architecture), available data (real, augmented, or synthetic), and optimization curricula to the target task and constraints. While KD routinely yields substantial runtime and memory gains with modest accuracy loss, open challenges remain in handling domain shift, rare-token transfer in NLP, optimization mismatch, and large-scale or privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques that transfer information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while preserving predictive performance. KD methods differ in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational structure) and how training proceeds (offline teacher supervision, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, or data-free synthesis). Practical deployments combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and require attention to teacher–student alignment, data availability, and task-specific choices. Empirical evidence shows KD reliably yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks, but success depends on optimization dynamics, the choice of distilled signals, and constraints such as access to original training data or deployment hardware.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other forms of teacher knowledge. Across vision and language tasks KD has enabled practical reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on what form of knowledge is transferred, how teacher and student representations are aligned, the availability and selection of data for distillation, and complementary compression techniques such as low-precision numerics, pruning, or architecture adaptation. Remaining challenges include optimization barriers that prevent exact teacher matching, reliable distillation without original data, robustness and fairness under compression, and principled methods for matching heterogeneous teacher–student pairs.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compress large neural models for deployment, while preserving performance and enabling new capabilities such as efficient federated learning, data-free compression, interpretability, and few-shot adaptation. Across architectures and tasks, KD variants—ranging from layer-to-layer alignment and progressive module replacement to meta-learned teachers and adversarial data synthesis—provide methods to trade computation, memory, and communication for small changes in accuracy. These methods make it possible to bring large pretrained models into production and edge settings, and to reconcile competing requirements such as privacy, heterogeneity, and interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit—logit-level supervision, intermediate-feature matching, layer-mapping, multi-teacher schedules, and data-aware or data-free variants—has been developed to meet deployment constraints in vision and natural language tasks. Empirical work shows that, when combined with architecture-aware choices and complementary compression techniques, KD frequently yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance, though careful method selection is required to mitigate mismatches, data limitations, and task-specific failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels — output logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure — and are commonly combined with architecture-level compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and training strategies (online co-training, curriculum schedules, synthetic-data protocols). Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while improving latency and memory usage, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and appropriate choice of transfer signal. Ongoing challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, aligning heterogeneous architectures, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, and operating in data-limited or privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Practical Extensions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students by transferring teacher knowledge during training. Beyond the original soft-target paradigm, a rich family of methods has emerged: feature- and attention-based matching, many-to-many layer alignment, self-distillation, and data- or representation-based distillation tailored to tasks such as object detection, translation, and pre-trained language model compression. KD also acts as a regularizer related to label smoothing and can be adapted to provide differential privacy, federated model aggregation, and improved adversarial robustness. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both the power of KD to improve student generalization and important limitations—optimization difficulties, mismatches in internal representations, and distributional effects on rare tokens or classes—that guide current research directions.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Work across vision and language shows a set of recurring strategies: transfer using softened outputs (soft targets), imitation of intermediate/internal representations, layer mapping between teacher and student, task-adaptive architecture search, self-distillation, and data-free distillation when original training data are unavailable. Empirical results indicate that properly designed distillation can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while offering large gains in inference speed and memory; however, success depends on which knowledge is transferred (outputs vs. internal features), how layers are aligned, and whether task specificity and data availability are addressed. The field currently balances practical engineering (architecture and search) with algorithmic refinements (losses and training regimes), and open challenges include robust data-free methods, principled many-to-many layer matching, and teacher designs that are optimized to be “student-friendly.”

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Bounded Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and natural language tasks. KD techniques — from logits matching to feature- and layer-level alignment, multi-teacher schedules, adversarial and data-free variants — enable large reductions in size and latency while retaining much of a teacher's performance. However, realizing these gains in practice requires task- and student-aware design choices, attention to data and privacy constraints, and explicit strategies to mitigate transferred fragilities. KD is therefore an essential tool in the compression toolbox, but not a universal remedy: careful method selection and evaluation under deployment constraints determine success.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, deployable models (students), or otherwise reduce network size while retaining performance. Approaches range from matching final predictions to aligning intermediate representations, and they address practical constraints such as limited data, privacy, device heterogeneity, and robustness. Recent work spans algorithmic mechanisms (soft targets, layer mapping, adversarial sample synthesis), application-specific pipelines (BERT compression, non-autoregressive translation, task-adaptive models), and theoretical interpretations that link distillation to regularization. This synthesis summarizes core techniques, practical extensions, and open challenges reported in recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques train compact student models to emulate larger teachers, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints across vision, speech, and language tasks. The body of work spans logits- or soft-target matching, feature- and layer-wise representation transfer, architecture-aware transformations, data-free and privacy-preserving methods, and multi-teacher or progressive schemes. Empirical and theoretical studies together show KD often improves student generalization and enables substantial efficiency gains, but outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution, and optimization choices. Practical pipelines combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search while addressing failure modes such as teacher errors, low-frequency token degradation, and domain shifts.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a core tool for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Evidence across vision, multimodal, and NLP tasks shows distillation can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling quantization, faster inference, and privacy-aware deployment. However, distillation is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, data unavailability, modality mismatches, and safety/robustness concerns can limit how closely a student can match its teacher. Combining complementary techniques—feature-level mimicry, intermediate-attention alignment, multi-teacher schedules, confidence-weighted losses, and generative or data-free strategies—yields the most reliable compressed models in practice.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones that remain useful in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings. When treated as a toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD supports a wide range of operational needs: output- and feature-level transfer, data- and teacher-aware strategies, privacy-preserving distributed training, and task-adaptive compression. Realizing KD’s benefits in production requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacity, and how to combine distillation with complementary methods such as architecture search, pruning, task-aware layer selection, and synthetic-data techniques.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses information from larger or more informative models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relations. Across vision and language tasks, KD variants (soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, self-distillation, ensemble-to-single transfer, and projector- or channel-aware alignment) have been shown to recover much of the teacher’s performance while enabling lower-latency and lower-memory deployment. Practical success depends on choosing what to transfer, tailoring objectives to the student architecture and target task, and addressing data availability and teacher imperfections. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, representative methods, empirical patterns, and open challenges for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable smaller or faster models to retain much of the performance of larger teachers by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or task-specific inductive biases. Work in this area spans supervised soft-target matching, intermediate-layer representation transfer, many-to-many layer alignment, data-free distillation, multi-teacher and ensemble-derived strategies, and online/distributed variants that exploit parallelism. Applications include compressing large pretrained language models for downstream NLP tasks, accelerating inference for computer vision and generative models, and producing interpretable or privacy-preserving compact models for healthcare and on-device deployment. Important trade-offs involve what form of knowledge is transferred (logits, activations, relations), access to training data, robustness to domain heterogeneity, and how to balance capacity, efficiency, and generalization in student models.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Compact, Robust, and Adaptable Deep Models in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers while enabling domain adaptation, deployment under resource constraints, privacy-preserving releases, and improved robustness. KD techniques span transfer from full teacher ensembles to single students, intermediate-layer alignment, self-distillation, and even data-free distillation; each variant addresses different operational constraints. However, distillation also carries risks (e.g., transfer of undesirable biases) and requires careful design choices (e.g., what information to transfer and what data to use). Combining advances across these variants yields effective, small NLP models fit for real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Crosby
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students that retain much of the teacher’s performance. KD spans soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, layer-aware alignment, self-distillation, and architecture-replacement strategies. When combined with appropriate pre-training, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture changes), KD enables practical tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, and memory for NLP and other modalities. Effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, what form of knowledge is transferred, and constraints such as data availability, privacy, fairness, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central to deploying deep neural networks in resource-constrained settings. The literature spans theoretical analyses of when and why distillation helps, practical algorithms for distilling logits, representations, and attention, techniques that require no original data, and adaptations for domains such as NLP, machine translation, and distributed training. Empirical work has shown KD can both accelerate inference and enable smaller models to approach or even exceed teacher performance in some settings, while recent advances address domain adaptivity, robustness, and teacher–student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and broadly applicable technique to compress large neural models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Work across computer vision, speech, and natural language processing demonstrates that KD can enable deployment of resource-efficient models, improve generalization in constrained settings, and be combined with other compression methods (e.g., low-precision numerics). At the same time, the field has identified important limitations and nuanced behaviors — such as data simplification effects, teacher–student mismatches, and domain or task-specific failure modes — that guide how KD should be applied in practice. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, variants, empirical benefits, and practical considerations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Recipe
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the first-line, practical strategy for compressing large models in deep learning and NLP because it provides a flexible set of mechanisms to transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from high-capacity teachers to smaller, efficient students. KD recovers much of teacher performance while reducing latency and memory footprint, and it composes naturally with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data synthesis). However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on what is distilled, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability, and robustness under domain shift or privacy constraints. A productive deployment strategy treats KD as the core of a hybrid pipeline, applies task-aware signal selection and layer alignment, uses multi- or student-aware teachers when appropriate, and combines distillation with lightweight model design and compression primitives to meet real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and compression seek to retain performance of large deep models while reducing size and latency for deployment. Methods extend beyond matching soft teacher outputs to include transferring internal representations, attention maps, and relational or adversarial signals; they can be applied during pretraining, task fine-tuning, or domain adaptation, and may operate with or without access to original training data. Empirical results across retrieval, reading comprehension, pretrained language models, and other domains show consistent trade-offs where careful choice of distillation targets, training curricula, and data augmentation materially improves student generalization and robustness while substantially lowering compute and memory requirements.

papers_seen.author: Bentley
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely used approach to compress large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. Research shows KD is a flexible toolkit: it can transfer final outputs (soft logits), intermediate representations, attention or relational signals, and can be combined with architectural compression (pruning, quantization) or training strategies (online distillation, multi-teacher schedules). Empirical successes span classification, retrieval, reading comprehension, and large-scale language modeling, but outcomes depend strongly on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization design. Important open problems include data-free distillation, cross-domain generalization, robustness and fairness preservation, and automated co-design of teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression: Powerful but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Its effectiveness arises from the ability to transfer different forms of knowledge (soft labels, intermediate features, attention, ensembles) and to combine distillation with data augmentation, pretraining, and task-aware objectives. However, KD is not uniformly successful: outcomes depend on teacher-student capacity alignment, the choice of distillation targets, data availability and augmentation strategy, and deployment constraints such as privacy or device heterogeneity. Careful selection of distillation signals, task-aware layer matching, and augmentation or synthetic-data strategies improve robustness; conversely, mismatches in architecture, domain shift, or heterogeneous federated settings can sharply limit benefits.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other forms of teacher knowledge. Across vision and language tasks KD has enabled practical reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on what form of knowledge is transferred, how teacher and student representations are aligned, the availability and selection of data for distillation, and complementary compression techniques such as low-precision numerics, pruning, or architecture adaptation. Remaining challenges include optimization barriers that prevent exact teacher matching, reliable distillation without original data, robustness and fairness under compression, and principled methods for matching heterogeneous teacher–student pairs.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones that remain useful in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings. When treated as a toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD supports a wide range of operational needs: output- and feature-level transfer, data- and teacher-aware strategies, privacy-preserving distributed training, and task-adaptive compression. Realizing KD’s benefits in production requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacity, and how to combine distillation with complementary methods such as architecture search, pruning, task-aware layer selection, and synthetic-data techniques.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller students that are deployable under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When applied thoughtfully—choosing what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, relational signals), aligning teacher and student architectures and tokenization, and combining KD with complementary techniques such as architecture search or targeted pruning—distillation routinely yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance and sometimes even improve generalization. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on data availability, teacher quality and friendliness, domain shifts, and the specific form of knowledge chosen for transfer. Effective deployment therefore requires principled design of the distillation objective, curricula or annealing schedules, and safeguards for robustness and rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural teachers into smaller student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision and language tasks, KD techniques include soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention- or relation-based alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher fusion, and data- or domain-aware variations. Empirical work shows that distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to meet deployment constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, available data, and training objectives. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, transferring robustness and inductive biases, and handling heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive environments.

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models to emulate larger teacher models so deployments meet latency, memory, or privacy constraints. KD encompasses a spectrum of signals to transfer—including softened outputs, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure—and integrates with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to produce efficient models. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often preserves large portions of teacher performance and can improve student generalization beyond mere compression, but outcomes depend strongly on what is distilled, teacher–student compatibility, access to data, and optimization choices. Practical pipelines therefore combine signal design, data strategies, and task-aware architecture choices to balance efficiency, robustness, and retained performance; open problems remain in data-free and privacy-preserving distillation, principled teacher design, and reliably transferring robustness and rare-token fidelity in sequence tasks.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A spectrum of distillation signals—soft logits, intermediate features and attention, relational/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher ensembles, and data- or privacy-aware synthesis—enables compact models that often retain most of teacher performance. Empirical results across NLP, speech, graph learning, and vision show KD’s practical value, while theoretical and empirical analyses point to mechanisms (soft-target regularization, ensemble-induced ‘‘dark knowledge’’, and representation shaping) and to limits tied to student capacity, data alignment, optimization dynamics, and robustness under distribution shift. Practical deployment requires careful selection of what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design).

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: Principled Use of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, practical method for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while retaining much of teacher performance. However, its success is conditional: choices about what to transfer, how to supervise internal representations, how to design student architectures for particular tasks, and how to handle data, distribution shift, and fairness constraints materially affect outcomes. I argue that KD should be treated as a flexible design pattern—combining soft-target transfer, internal-representation matching, task-adaptive architecture design, and explicit fairness or data strategies—to produce reliable, deployable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely applicable toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across vision and language tasks, KD has been adapted beyond simple soft-label matching to include intermediate-feature supervision, layer- or module-level mapping, selective sample transfer, data-free synthesis, and combinations with other compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical deployments reveal important dependencies on teacher quality, student architecture, data availability, and training protocols; when these are handled deliberately, distilled models can achieve strong trade-offs in accuracy, latency, and resource use. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data heterogeneity, preserving low-frequency or rare outputs, and aligning heterogeneous teacher–student architectures in privacy-sensitive or federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transform large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster, and more deployable models while attempting to preserve accuracy and useful inductive biases. Approaches span classic teacher–student logit matching, representation and feature imitation, layer mapping strategies for large pretrained language models, data-free and zero-shot methods that avoid access to original training data, and privacy- or communication-aware frameworks for distributed settings. Empirical work demonstrates these methods can yield practical speedups, substantial parameter reductions, and competitive task performance across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks; theoretical and empirical studies also clarify when softened teacher targets or distilled datasets best help student capacity. Remaining challenges include balancing privacy and utility, reducing the cost of distillation when teachers are large, and extending guarantees and methods across modalities and domain shifts.

papers_seen.author: Archer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Strategy Path for Compressing Deep Models in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across NLP and related domains. When paired with appropriate choices about what to transfer (logits, intermediate features, or higher-order ensemble signals), how to sample or synthesize training data, and how to design student architectures and training curricula, distillation can preserve much of the teacher’s performance while reducing memory, compute, and latency. However, its success depends on data access and quality, teacher–student alignment, and training protocols; therefore, distillation is best applied as part of a considered pipeline that includes augmentation, selective sample use, and—when needed—data-free synthesis or multi-teacher strategies to meet practical constraints.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD variants transfer information via softened outputs, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals, and adversarially or synthetically generated inputs. When combined with architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, or data strategies, KD supports deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, success depends on careful matching of what is transferred to student capacity, handling data scarcity or distribution shift, and mitigating propagation of teacher errors. This synthesis summarizes common mechanisms, representative algorithmic families, empirical patterns, and actionable recommendations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. It generalizes from soft-target supervision to intermediate-representation matching, multi-teacher ensembles, and data-free synthesis. When combined with complementary strategies (pre-training of compact models, data augmentation, pruning, and hardware-aware layout), KD enables substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while largely preserving task performance. Realizing these gains requires careful choices about what knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to handle limited or sensitive data; when these are addressed, KD serves as a reliable foundation for practical compression pipelines in NLP and other domains.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compress large neural models into smaller, more deployable ones while preserving much of their performance. Contemporary work shows KD is not a single algorithm but a family of techniques that transfer knowledge via soft labels, intermediate feature supervision, layer-wise mappings, data augmentation, and even data-free synthesis. KD has been applied across modalities and tasks — from compressing large language and multimodal transformers to enabling lightweight generative models and resource-efficient inference on edge devices. Empirical and theoretical analyses have begun to explain when and why distillation works, how it transfers inductive biases, and which input-side interventions (e.g., mixup/CutMix variants) improve transfer. Practical challenges remain in aligning heterogeneous teacher–student architectures, operating under limited or private data, and deciding what form of teacher knowledge (logits, features, relations, or structural priors) best serves a given student architecture.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models to mimic larger teacher models so that deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints becomes feasible. KD methods transfer different forms of information — soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure — and are often combined with architectural compression, data augmentation, or privacy-preserving mechanisms. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can improve generalization beyond mere compression, but outcomes depend strongly on what is distilled, teacher–student compatibility, access to (or synthesis of) data, and optimization choices. Practical pipelines therefore blend signal design (logits vs. features), data strategies, and task-aware architecture choices to balance efficiency and retained performance.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expressive models to smaller, efficient models to enable practical deployment without excessive loss in performance. These methods include matching teacher soft outputs, feature-level alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and architecture-aware strategies for heterogeneous settings. Across domains—vision, speech, NLP, and recommender systems—distillation is used both to compress models for latency and memory constraints and to inject complementary knowledge (e.g., cross-task or cross-modal signals). Empirical work shows that careful design choices (e.g., mixing hard/soft targets, projector modules, or student-aware teacher training) and task-specific adaptations address common pitfalls such as information loss on rare tokens or domain shifts. Open directions include stronger theoretical understanding, robustness under imperfect teachers, and principled integration with quantization, federated settings, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, expressive models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple logit-matching to a diverse toolkit that includes feature- and layer-level supervision, multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, self-distillation and teacher optimization, and approaches that enable data-free or privacy-preserving compression. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling faster inference and smaller footprints; however, practical success depends on choices about objectives, alignment between teacher and student, data availability, and robustness to domain shift. Open directions include stronger theoretical characterization of what is transferred, principled treatment of heterogeneous teachers, and tighter integration of KD with quantization, pruning, and privacy mechanisms.
